theme: Manasseh; Josiah’s reform; the Book of the Law found
readingInstruction: Read 2 Kings 21:1-23:37. Judah’s worst king is followed by one of its best, and yet the judgment does not turn back. Read chapter 22 slowly, and notice what happens when the Book of the Law is found.
settingTheScene: This unit begins the last chapter of Judah’s story. Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, the longest of any king, and the Bible calls his reign the cause of Judah’s fall. His grandson Josiah then led the greatest reform in the nation’s history, and still the sentence of exile stood. Jeremiah began to prophesy in Josiah’s thirteenth year, so the prophet you are about to meet stands inside this story.
observation: Manasseh “did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, according to the despicable practices of the nations” (21:2).
He “burned his son as an offering” and “shed very much innocent blood” (21:6, 16).
“I am bringing such disaster upon Jerusalem and Judah that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle” (21:12).
Josiah “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD” at eight years old (22:1-2).
“I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD” (22:8).
“When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes” (22:11).
“Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before the LORD… I also have heard you” (22:19).
“Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart… Still the LORD did not turn from the burning of his great anger” (23:25-26).
interpretation:
Manasseh rebuilt the high places, set up altars to the host of heaven inside the temple courts, practiced sorcery, and sacrificed his own son. The writer says he led the people astray to do more evil than the nations God had destroyed before Israel. The sentence given in chapter 21 is clear: Jerusalem will be wiped out like a dish turned upside down.

Then Josiah. When the Book of the Law is found during temple repairs, it has been lost so long that its words come as a shock. The king hears it read and tears his clothes. This is the right response to Scripture: not curiosity but fear and humility. God tells him that judgment will come, but not in his days, because his heart was tender.

Josiah then does everything the book requires. He reads it to all the people and renews the covenant. He tears down the high places, destroys the altars, defiles Topheth where children were burned, and keeps the greatest Passover since the judges. The writer gives him the highest praise: no king turned to the LORD with all his heart, soul, and might like him.

And yet. “Still the LORD did not turn from the burning of his great anger.” Reform could slow the judgment but could not undo a generation’s habits. The people had cleaned the house, but their hearts had not changed. That is the problem the rest of this unit will face, and why Jeremiah will promise a covenant written on the heart. Josiah dies at Megiddo in 609 BC, and within a few years the nation is under Egypt and then Babylon.
connection: Jesus rebuked leaders who “neglect the weightier matters of the law” (Matthew 23:23). Hebrews 8:7-13 says that the first covenant was faulty because the people did not continue in it, and quotes Jeremiah’s promise of a new one. Romans 7:7-25 shows the law exposing sin without being able to change the heart. Luke 4:17 shows Jesus finding the scroll of Isaiah and reading, a better finding of the Word.
application:
Open your Bible today as if you had just found it. Ask what you would do if you really heard it.

Consider whether you have been tidying up outward habits while your heart stays the same.

Pray for a tender heart, one that trembles at God’s word.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to make you tremble at his word as Josiah did.
Ask him not to let you settle for outward reform.
Confess where your heart has been hard.
